walkthroughs.title: Seeds, a model that references them and rows rejected by a cast

steps.excerpt:
import json
import os
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import duckdb
import yaml
steps.title: Imports
steps.explanation: json reads dbt's artifact files, tempfile and pathlib manage a throwaway folder, duckdb queries the warehouse file directly and yaml writes dbt's configuration. dbt itself is imported later, inside invoke.
steps.observe: Nothing here touches the network.

steps.title: A self contained dbt project
steps.explanation: project builds a complete, throwaway dbt project inside a temporary folder. It disables telemetry and colors, creates the standard models, seeds, snapshots and macros folders, and writes dbt_project.yml. The profile points dbt at a local DuckDB file with one thread and a 256 MB memory limit, so everything runs offline and stays small. Callers pass dictionaries of model SQL, seed CSV text and optional YAML, and the helper writes each one to the right file.
steps.observe: After project returns, the folder holds a project dbt can build, plus the model and seed files you passed in.

steps.excerpt:
def invoke(root, *arguments, succeeds=True):
    from dbt.cli.main import dbtRunner

    result = dbtRunner().invoke(
        [
            "--quiet",
            "--no-use-colors",
            "--no-send-anonymous-usage-stats",
            *arguments,
            "--project-dir",
            str(root),
            "--profiles-dir",
            str(root),
            "--no-partial-parse",
        ]
    )
    if succeeds:
        assert result.success, str(result.exception)
    else:
        assert not result.success, "The deliberately invalid fixture was accepted."
    return result
steps.title: Run dbt from Python
steps.explanation: invoke runs dbt from Python with dbtRunner instead of a shell command. The flags keep output quiet, turn off colors and usage stats, point dbt at this project and skip partial parsing so every run reads the files fresh. succeeds lets a test demand either success or a deliberate failure, so a broken fixture cannot silently pass.
steps.observe: A failed build raises an AssertionError that carries dbt's own exception text.

steps.title: Read results back
steps.explanation: rows opens the DuckDB file and runs a SQL query, so the test checks real tables, not dbt's log messages. artifact loads a JSON file from dbt's target folder, such as manifest.json, which describes every node dbt knows about.
steps.observe: Checking the database directly is stronger evidence than reading dbt's success message.

steps.title: Seed, model and build
steps.explanation: The seed raw_orders is a CSV with three rows. The orders model selects from it with {{ ref('raw_orders') }}, which tells dbt about the dependency so it loads the seed first. dbt build loads seeds, builds models and runs tests in dependency order. The manifest confirms the seed was registered as a seed node.
steps.observe: The orders table has 3 rows and amounts summing to 21.

steps.title: Rejecting a bad value without failing the load
steps.explanation: Now one amount is the text bad. try_cast returns NULL instead of erroring, and the WHERE clause drops rows where the cast failed. The raw seed still has all three rows, so the rejected row remains visible for investigation instead of disappearing.
steps.observe: clean holds ids 1 and 3; raw_orders still holds 3 rows, one of which fails the cast.

steps.title: Print results and the pass marker
steps.explanation: main prints both dictionaries and the marker line after every assert succeeds.
steps.observe: The last line is dbt-002 reference checks passed.

walkthroughs.title: Incremental models, watermarks and why late events need a full refresh

steps.title: The shared project helper
steps.explanation: project builds a complete, throwaway dbt project inside a temporary folder. It disables telemetry and colors, creates the standard models, seeds, snapshots and macros folders, and writes dbt_project.yml. The profile points dbt at a local DuckDB file with one thread and a 256 MB memory limit, so everything runs offline and stays small. Callers pass dictionaries of model SQL, seed CSV text and optional YAML, and the helper writes each one to the right file.
steps.observe: This is the same helper used across the track; only the models and seeds change per example.

steps.title: Run dbt and query DuckDB
steps.explanation: invoke runs dbt from Python with dbtRunner instead of a shell command. The flags keep output quiet, turn off colors and usage stats, point dbt at this project and skip partial parsing so every run reads the files fresh. succeeds lets a test demand either success or a deliberate failure, so a broken fixture cannot silently pass. rows then reads query results straight from the DuckDB file.
steps.observe: Each invoke call is one full dbt command, such as build or run.

steps.excerpt:
def example_one():
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
        sql = (
            "{{ config(materialized='incremental') }}\n"
            "select *\n"
            "from {{ ref('events') }}\n"
            "{% if is_incremental() %} where updated_at > (select max(updated_at) from {{ this }}) "
            "{% endif %}"
        )
steps.title: An incremental model with a watermark
steps.explanation: materialized='incremental' tells dbt to add rows to an existing table instead of rebuilding it. is_incremental() is false on the first run and true afterward. When true, the WHERE clause keeps only events with updated_at greater than the largest value already stored, which is called a watermark. {{ this }} refers to the model's own existing table.
steps.observe: On the first run the filter is skipped and every row is loaded.

steps.excerpt:
p = project(d, models={"history": sql}, seeds={"events": "id,updated_at,amount\n1,10,5\n"})
        invoke(p, "build")
        (p / "seeds/events.csv").write_text("id,updated_at,amount\n1,10,5\n2,20,7\n")
        invoke(p, "build")
        invoke(p, "run")
        assert rows(p, "select id,amount from history order by id") == [(1, 5), (2, 7)]
        return {"monotone_append_rows": 2, "rerun_did_not_duplicate": True}
steps.title: Append a newer row, then rerun
steps.explanation: The first build loads one event. The seed file is then rewritten with a second, newer event and built again, so only the new row passes the watermark. A further run with no new data adds nothing, which shows the model is safe to rerun.
steps.observe: history contains exactly ids 1 and 2, with no duplicates.

steps.excerpt:
def example_two():
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
        sql = (
            "{{ config(materialized='incremental') }}\n"
            "select *\n"
            "from {{ ref('events') }}\n"
            "{% if is_incremental() %} where updated_at > (select max(updated_at) from {{ this }}) "
            "{% endif %}"
        )
        p = project(
            d, models={"history": sql}, seeds={"events": "id,updated_at,amount\n1,10,5\n2,20,7\n"}
        )
        invoke(p, "build")
        (p / "seeds/events.csv").write_text("id,updated_at,amount\n1,10,5\n2,20,7\n3,15,9\n")
        invoke(p, "build")
        assert rows(p, "select count(*) from history") == [(2,)]
steps.title: A late event slips under the watermark
steps.explanation: This time the new event has updated_at 15, which is older than the stored maximum of 20. The incremental filter rejects it, so the table still has two rows even though the source has three. This is the core risk of timestamp watermarks.
steps.observe: history has 2 rows while the source seed has 3.

steps.title: Recover with a full refresh
steps.explanation: dbt run --full-refresh drops the incremental logic for one run and rebuilds the table from all source rows, so the late event is finally included.
steps.observe: After the refresh history has 3 rows.

steps.title: Print results and the pass marker
steps.explanation: main prints both dictionaries and the marker line.
steps.observe: The last line is dbt-008 reference checks passed.

            str(root),

def names(result):
    return [str(value) for value in result.result]
steps.title: Run dbt and collect node names
steps.explanation: invoke runs dbt from Python with dbtRunner instead of a shell command. The flags keep output quiet, turn off colors and usage stats, point dbt at this project and skip partial parsing so every run reads the files fresh. succeeds lets a test demand either success or a deliberate failure, so a broken fixture cannot silently pass. names turns the result of dbt ls into a list of plain strings.
steps.observe: dbt ls only lists nodes; it builds nothing.

steps.title: Three models, one tagged
steps.explanation: base carries the tag feature through its config block. child depends on base through ref. unrelated has no link to either. dbt parse reads the project and writes manifest.json without running any SQL.
steps.observe: The project graph is base to child, plus a separate unrelated node.

steps.title: Graph selection with tag:feature+
steps.explanation: tag:feature selects models with that tag, and the trailing plus adds everything downstream. --resource-type model and --output name keep the listing to model names. The selection includes child because it depends on base, and excludes unrelated.
steps.observe: dbt prints base and child, and the function returns them sorted.

steps.title: Save state, then change a model
steps.explanation: After parsing, the manifest is copied into previous_state. That copy is the baseline. Rewriting base.sql changes base's definition relative to the baseline.
steps.observe: Only base.sql was edited; child.sql is unchanged.

steps.excerpt:
selected = names(
            invoke(
                p,
                "ls",
                "--state",
                str(state),
                "--select",
                "state:modified+",
                "--resource-type",
                "model",
                "--output",
                "name",
            )
        )
        assert set(selected) == {"base", "child"}, selected
        return {
            "changed_and_downstream": sorted(selected),
            "state_is_not_a_quality_certificate": True,
        }
steps.title: state:modified+ finds the change and its consumers
steps.explanation: --state points dbt at the saved manifest, and state:modified+ selects nodes whose definition differs plus everything downstream. That is how continuous integration can rebuild only what a change affects. The returned flag records an important limit: a state comparison says what changed, not whether the change is correct.
steps.observe: The selection is base and child again, this time because of the edit.

steps.title: Print results and the pass marker
steps.explanation: main prints both dictionaries and the marker line after every check passes. dbt ls also writes the selected names, which is why base and child appear on their own lines.
steps.observe: The last line is dbt-013 reference checks passed.
